statement: At one Colorado university hospital's emergency department, 2012 to 2016, clinicians judged 2,567 visits (visits, not people) to be at least partly due to cannabis; 238 (9.3%) were recorded as edible and 2,329 as inhaled (135 of these had no route written down and were counted as inhaled). Compared with inhaled visits, edible visits more often involved intoxication (48.3% against 27.8%; difference 20.5 percentage points, 95% CI 13.9 to 27.1), acute psychiatric symptoms (18.0% against 10.9%; 7.1, 2.1 to 12.1) and cardiovascular symptoms (8.0% against 3.1%; 4.9, 1.4 to 8.4), and less often gastrointestinal symptoms (15.1% against 32.3%; cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4% against 18.0%) or admission to hospital (18.9% against 32.9%); psychiatric symptoms of any kind were similar (26.1% against 24.5%). Severe heart events (heart attack, dangerous heart rhythm) occurred in both groups, with no counts given. Because edibles were under a tenth of the visits, most visits for each of these reasons were inhaled (647 of 762 intoxication visits, 254 of 297 acute psychiatric visits, 73 of 92 cardiovascular visits; editors' arithmetic from the table counts), and the authors write that, given how often inhaled visits occurred and led to admission, education about inhaled cannabis may have the greatest public-health effect. The two groups also differed in who they were (women 51.3% against 33.1%; living outside Colorado 40.8% against 6.6%); a 2016 letter from the same hospital group, cited second-hand in the overview described below and not read, reported that edible-related visits by out-of-state patients rose from 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits between 2013 and 2014, with no significant change for Colorado residents. Against Colorado sales in 2014 to 2016, edibles were 10.7% of this hospital's attributable visits but 0.32% of THC sold by weight, under assumed product contents; the authors call this about 33 times the share expected if the routes were equally likely to lead to a visit, and list its limits (assumed contents, one hospital set against statewide sales, home-grown and illicit supply not counted). A 2016 narrative overview (no stated search or appraisal of studies; its figures are second-hand) quotes another measure, edible units at about 45 percent of Colorado cannabis sales in 2014, without saying how sales were counted, so any such ratio depends on the denominator chosen. No source read here timed effects in patients. The hospital paper and the overview both describe, citing pharmacology work that was not read here, a later and longer effect after eating THC than after inhaling it (the overview: a start within minutes of inhaling against 30 to 90 minutes after eating; the hospital paper: clearance within about 4 hours against about 12). The overview adds that more of the active product 11-OH-THC reaches the blood after eating, which it says may account for stronger, longer-lasting effects; that blood THC after eating is lower than after smoking and tracks intoxication differently from person to person; and that this variation and the delay may lead people to take more than intended before the effect starts, which its abstract says often results in profoundly adverse effects (no count given). The hospital paper cites a consumer survey and an analysis of Twitter posts (neither read) in which people report longer-lasting effects with edibles than with smoking or vaping, and more intense effects and unpleasant psychiatric symptoms. The overview relays anecdotal reports from patients, including patients who took cannabis daily, of eating a whole product after feeling no effect from a first serving, and describes one death in Colorado in 2014 (a 19-year-old man; the autopsy named cannabis intoxication a chief contributing factor) after he ate the whole cookie within two hours of a first serving, having not felt intoxicated within an hour (a public-health case report, as cited). The hospital paper cites three deaths linked to edibles from news reports; none of its 2,567 visits ended in death. No source read here counts how often people eat more after a slow start. What these sources cannot show: how many people took each form (shares of visits are not the chance that a form leads to a visit); who took which form (no adjustment); how much was eaten (a dose was charted for 130 of the 2,567 visits, 80 of them edible; the authors could not verify doses, say eaten doses may have been larger than inhaled ones, and were surprised that the charted edible doses were low); what the products contained (not tested; the overview reports second-hand, from a test of medicinal edibles not read here, that most differed from their labels); and what happened to people who took cannabis without harm or did not attend hospital (the authors note that most people who take cannabis may have no adverse effect). Route came from chart notes and patients' own accounts, and the authors say counting undocumented routes as inhaled could bias toward more illness in the inhaled group. Inhaled visits were not split by product (flower, vaped oil, concentrates) or checked for tobacco mixed in, and no comparison was made with people who do not use cannabis. The overview states that edible products account for most health-care visits for cannabis intoxication, citing a 2015 viewpoint not read here; the hospital count has edibles at 115 of 762 intoxication visits (15.1%). The overview also infers that eating cannabis does not seem to affect lung function or cancer risk, citing no study of people who eat cannabis, and nothing read here compares the lungs of people who eat cannabis with those who smoke it. Follow-up was the visit itself: the hospital data do not follow anyone afterwards, and the overview has no data of its own. For children, the overview gives only second-hand figures (poison-centre calls, and one children's hospital, rising over 2005 to 2015) and says emergency visits for children remain relatively low. Funding as printed: the hospital paper, the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (competitive grant; the paper says the funder had no part in design, analysis, interpretation or dissemination), with the first author's NIH support and membership of the Colorado Retail Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee; the overview, RTI International internal funds and a US National Institute on Drug Abuse grant, with no conflict statement printed. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding is printed for either.
plain: At one big Colorado hospital, 2,567 emergency visits over five years were judged to be at least partly due to cannabis. Only 238 of them, about 1 in 11, were linked to eating or drinking cannabis; the rest were linked to smoking or vaping it. Compared with the smoking and vaping visits, the edible visits more often involved being very intoxicated, sudden mental-health symptoms such as acute anxiety or psychosis, or heart symptoms, and less often involved vomiting or being admitted to hospital. But because far more visits involved smoking or vaping, most visits for each of those problems still involved smoking or vaping. Two papers describe a slower start and a longer-lasting effect from eating cannabis than from inhaling it, and some case reports describe people eating more after feeling nothing at first, but no study here timed effects in patients or counted how often people eat more. The papers could not count how many people took each form, how much they took, what was in the product, or who never went to hospital, so they cannot say how likely any form is to lead to a hospital visit, and they did not compare either form with people who do not use cannabis.
population: 2,567 emergency visits (median age 30; 65.2% male; 9.8% from outside Colorado) to one Colorado university hospital, 2012 to 2016, that clinicians judged at least partly due to cannabis: 238 recorded as edible and 2,329 as inhaled. Visits, not people (for example, 301 people accounted for 440 of the visits for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome). Timing and case-report material comes from a 2016 narrative overview citing laboratory studies and case reports (not read).
exposure: Cannabis recorded in the chart as eaten or drunk (edible; 238 visits), from the nursing questionnaire and providers' notes, self-reported and unverified; a dose was charted for 80 of the 238 (study measure only); product contents not tested.
comparator: Visits recorded as inhaled (2,194 documented as smoked or otherwise inhaled, plus 135 with no route written down, counted as inhaled) at the same hospital in the same years. No comparison group of people who took each form and did not attend hospital, and no comparison with people who do not use cannabis; for the sales comparison, flower and edible units sold in Colorado in 2014 to 2016 under assumed THC contents.
outcome: Reasons for the visit coded from the chart (intoxication; acute, acute-on-chronic and chronic psychiatric symptoms; gastrointestinal symptoms including cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome; cardiovascular symptoms), admission and length of stay; the later and longer effect after eating as described from cited pharmacology and case reports, not measured in patients.
magnitude: Hospital chart review (Monte 2019), share of each group's visits, edible-attributed (n = 238) against inhaled-attributed (n = 2,329), % (difference in percentage points, 95% CI): intoxication 48.3 vs 27.8 (20.5; 13.9 to 27.1); acute psychiatric symptoms 18.0 vs 10.9 (7.1; 2.1 to 12.1); cardiovascular symptoms 8.0 vs 3.1 (4.9; 1.4 to 8.4); any psychiatric symptom 26.1 vs 24.5 (1.6; -4.2 to 7.4); gastrointestinal symptoms 15.1 vs 32.3 (-17.2; -22.1 to -12.2), of which cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4 vs 18.0 (-9.6; -13.5 to -5.7); admitted 18.9 vs 32.9; women 51.3 vs 33.1; living outside Colorado 40.8 vs 6.6 (each P < 0.001); median length of stay 2 hours (range 1 to 54) vs 3 hours (0 to 121). Severe heart events (myocardial infarction, ventricular dysrhythmia) in both groups, no counts. Edible-attributed visits as a share of all visits for each reason, editors' arithmetic from Table 2 counts: intoxication 115 of 762 (15.1%), acute psychiatric 43 of 297 (14.5%), cardiovascular 19 of 92 (20.7%); edible 238 of 2,567 visits (9.3%). Route recorded in 2,432 of 2,567 visits (94.7%); dose charted in 130 (5.1%), 80 of them edible, 19 of those at 50 mg of THC or more (as charted, unverified; study measure only). Eight symptom groups compared, no correction for multiple comparisons. Colorado sales 2014 to 2016: 219 edible and 1,819 inhaled attributable visits (edible 10.7%); edible 0.32% of THC sold by weight (flower 327,990 kg at an assumed 20% THC; 21.2 million edible units at an assumed 10 mg each); flower-to-edible THC ratio 309 (range 279 to 325); visit share about 33 times the share expected if both routes were equally likely to lead to a visit (authors). Overview (Barrus 2016, narrative, second-hand figures): Colorado 2014 edible units 1.96 million medicinal and 2.85 million retail, said to be about 45 percent of total cannabis sales (measure not stated); timing as cited, inhaled start within minutes and effects tapering within 2 to 3 hours, eaten start 30 to 90 minutes and peak 2 to 4 hours after eating (hospital paper, from the same pharmacology review: clearance about 4 hours after inhaling, about 12 hours after eating); oral bioavailability 6 to 10 percent of the amount in the product (as cited); 83 percent of tested medicinal edibles more than 10 percent from their labelled THC (second-hand, not read); out-of-state patients' edible-related visits 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits, 2013 to 2014 (second-hand, not read).

evidence.locator: Abstract; Results, 1st (unlabelled) paragraph; Methods › Study Participants and Coding, paragraph; Methods › Measurements, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Chart review of all emergency visits to one Colorado university hospital, 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2016: 449,031 eligible visits, 9,973 with a cannabis-related diagnosis code (the participants were adults with such a code), 2,567 (25.7% of the 9,973) judged at least partly attributable to cannabis. Route was recorded in 2,432 of the 2,567 (94.7%): 238 edible (9.3% of the 2,567; 9.8% of the 2,432) and 2,194 inhaled; the 135 visits with insufficient documentation were counted as inhaled, giving 2,329. A dose was recorded in 130 (5.1%). Cannabis use is assessed in the nursing assessment questionnaire and the providers' notes; the route was captured from the medical record, and inhalation was presumed when it was not documented. Visits attributable to inhaled and to edible cannabis both rose each year (Figure 2, an image, not read).

evidence.locator: Table 2; Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 2nd paragraph; Abstract
evidence.extracted: Table 2, edible-attributed (n = 238) against inhaled-attributed (n = 2,329) visits, % (difference in percentage points, 95% CI): intoxication 48.3 vs 27.8 (20.5; 13.9 to 27.1); acute psychiatric symptoms 18.0 vs 10.9 (7.1; 2.1 to 12.1); cardiovascular symptoms 8.0 vs 3.1 (4.9; 1.4 to 8.4); any psychiatric symptom 26.1 vs 24.5 (1.6; -4.2 to 7.4); gastrointestinal symptoms 15.1 vs 32.3 (-17.2; -22.1 to -12.2); cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4 vs 18.0 (-9.6; -13.5 to -5.7). The text adds that severe adverse cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction and ventricular dysrhythmia, occurred in both groups; no counts are given. Only two route groups appear in the tables and text, edible and inhaled; the inhaled group is not broken down by product, and tobacco mixed into joints is not recorded.

evidence.locator: Table 2, counts; Results › Reasons for Cannabis-Attributable ED Visits, paragraph
evidence.extracted: Table 2 counts, edible and inhaled: intoxication 115 and 647 (762 in all); acute psychiatric symptoms 43 and 254 (297); cardiovascular symptoms 19 and 73 (92); gastrointestinal symptoms 36 and 752; cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 20 and 420. Editors' arithmetic: edible-attributed visits were 15.1%, 14.5% and 20.7% of the intoxication, acute psychiatric and cardiovascular visits, so most visits for those reasons were inhaled-attributed. Across the 2,567 visits (reasons not mutually exclusive): gastrointestinal symptoms including cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 788 (30.7%), of which cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 440 visits (17.1%) by 301 people; intoxication 762 (29.7%), psychiatric symptoms 633 (24.7%), cardiovascular symptoms 92 (3.6%).

evidence.locator: Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Discussion, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Edible-attributed against inhaled-attributed visits: women 51.3% vs 33.1%; living outside Colorado 40.8% vs 6.6%; admitted 18.9% vs 32.9% (each P < 0.001); median length of stay 2 hours (range 1 to 54) vs 3 hours (0 to 121); age similar, no figures. Table 1, all 2,567 attributable visits: median age 30; 65.2% male; 9.8% from outside Colorado; 31.6% admitted, 62.5% discharged, 2.1% transferred to a psychiatric facility, no deaths. The Discussion says the higher admission rate in the inhaled group seemed driven by admission of patients with cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome; this is not analysed.

The authors write that, although less frequent overall, edible products lead to more acute psychiatric events and cardiovascular symptoms than inhaled exposure, and that the high frequency of visits and the greater likelihood of admission with inhalable products suggest that education about the adverse health effects of inhalable cannabis may have the greatest effect on public health.

evidence.locator: Results › Colorado Sales Data by Route of Exposure; Table 3; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Colorado sales, 2014 to 2016 (Table 3): 219 edible-attributed and 1,819 inhaled-attributed visits, so edibles were 10.7% of attributable visits, against 0.32% of THC sold by weight (flower 327,990 kg at an assumed 20% THC; 21.2 million edible units at an assumed 10 mg each; ratio of flower to edible THC 309, range 279 to 325). The authors call the observed share about 33 times higher than expected if both routes were equally toxic and say careful interpretation is required: THC content was assumed, one hospital was compared with state-level sales, home-grown and black-market cannabis were not counted, and sales are not geocoded.

Limits stated by the authors: retrospective design with exposure captured largely through self-report; no comparative community-based exposure cohort; patients presenting to the emergency department differ from the overall population of people who use cannabis, most of whom may have no adverse effects, so a prospective cohort of people who use cannabis and people who do not is needed; doses could not be verified and ingested doses may have been larger than inhaled doses. A dose was documented in 80 edible-attributed visits and in 19 it was 50 mg or higher; the authors were surprised by the low edible doses reported, given the THC content of a typical Colorado joint. Route was presumed inhaled when not documented, which they say could have biased the analyses toward greater toxicity in the inhaled group. The hospital has the second most visits per year in the state and is in an area of high cannabis availability.

Timing as described by the authors, citing a pharmacology review (Grotenhermen 2003, not read): inhaled cannabis gives clinical effects within 10 minutes, a peak blood concentration within 30 to 90 minutes and complete clearance within 4 hours; oral THC does not reach a significant blood concentration until at least 30 minutes, peaks at about 3 hours and clears about 12 hours after ingestion. People report longer-lasting effects with edibles than with smoking or vaping (reference 8, Giombi 2018, on consumers' perceptions of edibles; its design is not stated on the page) and more intense effects and unpleasant psychiatric symptoms (reference 9, an analysis of Twitter posts); neither was read. Death has been associated with edible products in three cases taken from news reports (references 10 to 12). No timing was measured in this study's patients.

evidence.locator: Methods › Role of the Funding Source, paragraph; Grant Support, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Funded by a competitive grant from the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment for a project on the adverse health effects of edible cannabis products; the paper states that the department was not involved in study design, analysis, data interpretation or dissemination. The first author received support from NIH K23 GM110516, NIH CTSI UL1 TR001082 and CDPHE 17 FHHA 96950 (Grant Support). Disclosures: the first author reports grants from the department during the study and sits on the Colorado Retail Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee, a group of clinicians and scientists reviewing the literature on the public health effects of cannabis; another author reports department grants; authors not named disclosed no conflicts. No cannabis-industry, tobacco-industry or advocacy funding is printed.

A narrative overview published by RTI Press (PMC lists it as Methods Rep RTI Press), written for the educated layperson and policy makers. The Abstract says little research has evaluated how ingestion differs from other methods of cannabis use in therapeutic efficacy, subjective effects and safety; that the most prominent difference between ingestion and inhalation of cannabis extracts is the delayed onset of drug effect with ingestion; and that consumers who do not understand this may consume more than intended before the effect starts, often resulting in profoundly adverse effects (no count is given). The Introduction says the authors describe promises and challenges and critically examine extant research; no search method, selection criteria or appraisal of studies is described.

In Colorado in 2014, 1.96 million units of edible medicinal cannabis-infused products and 2.85 million units of edible retail products were sold, which the authors say accounted for about 45 percent of the total cannabis sales in the state (a state report, as cited); the measure of sales is not stated. Homemade edibles are not tracked, and the data show sales and not the proportion of people who consume edibles.

After eating, liver first-pass metabolism forms 11-OH-THC, a potent psychoactive metabolite that appears in blood in higher quantities after ingestion than after inhalation (as cited); the authors write that it may be responsible for the stronger and longer-lasting effect of edibles compared with comparable doses of smoked cannabis. Inhaled THC takes initial effect within minutes and shows peak effect in about 20 to 30 minutes, with psychoactive effects tapering off within 2 to 3 hours; the initial psychoactive effect of edibles takes 30 to 90 minutes to be felt and the high is longer-lasting, with a peak 2 to 4 hours after ingestion (Grotenhermen 2003 and others, as cited, not read). Weight, metabolism, gender and eating habits are said to affect how soon and how long.

After oral doses, plasma THC is lower than after smoking or infusion, and its correlation with degree of intoxication varies considerably across individuals (Hollister 1981, as cited); oral bioavailability is 6 to 10 percent of the amount in the product (Schwilke 2009, as cited). The authors say the lack of consistency and the delayed intoxication may lead both new and experienced people to take more than intended, and write that edible products are responsible for the majority of health care visits due to cannabis intoxication, which they say is likely due to users' failure to appreciate the delayed effects (a 2015 JAMA article by Monte, Zane and Heard, as cited, not read).
evidence.quote: responsible for the majority of health care visits due to cannabis intoxication

evidence.extracted: Dosage estimation for retail products may be inexact (Vandrey 2015, as cited). Anecdotal reports from medicinal cannabis patients are said to confirm that even people who take cannabis daily may consume more than expected (Hudak 2015, a letter in the American Journal of Psychiatry, as cited): having eaten the suggested serving first, patients ate the entire product after not feeling any effects, and found it practical to eat the entire product in one sitting.

One death after an edible is described: in March 2014 a 19-year-old man died of injuries from jumping from a fourth-floor balcony in Colorado after eating a cannabis-infused cookie (a public-health case report, as cited). The text says he was told to eat one serving, and that having not felt intoxicated within 60 minutes he ate the whole cookie within 2 hours of that serving; the autopsy identified cannabis intoxication as a chief contributing factor.

A 2014 newspaper investigation found the actual THC content of retail edibles often differed significantly from labels; from mid-2014 Colorado required THC in recreational edibles to be tested and labelled but tested only against a threshold, which does not check label accuracy. One study of medicinal edibles sold in California and Washington is reported to have found that the total THC content of 83 percent of edibles tested differed from the labelled amounts by over 10 percent, with more than half containing significantly less than claimed and nearly a quarter significantly more (Vandrey 2015, as cited; not read).

evidence.locator: Challenges of Edibles, 10th, 11th and 12th paragraphs; reference list (Kim 2016)
evidence.extracted: Children: in a review of US poison-centre data on unintentional exposures in young children (up to 9 years of age), cannabis-related calls rose 30.3 percent a year in decriminalized states, 11.5 percent in states undergoing transition to decriminalization and 1.5 percent in nonlegal states, 2005 to 2011 (Wang 2014, as cited), with similar increases in edible-related calls in 2013 to 2015 (Cao 2016, as cited). The authors write that emergency visits for child exposure remain relatively low: a Colorado children's hospital saw no cases of accidental ingestion in 2005 to 2009, eight children who ingested edible cannabis in 2013 and 14 in 2014 (a hospital-association web item, as cited). Visitors: out-of-town patient visits to an Aurora, Colorado hospital for problems after edibles almost doubled from 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits between 2013 and 2014, with no significant difference for Colorado residents (Kim 2016, as cited; not read); that study's authors attributed the rise to higher potency and visitors' unfamiliarity with edibles. The reference list gives the letter's authors as Kim, Hall, Genco, Van Dyke, Barker and Monte (the first author of Monte 2019 is Monte).

On smoke: cannabis and tobacco smoke are said to be similar in kind in toxicity; cannabis smoke is linked to lung inflammation and bronchitis; the link to chronic lung disease is unclear; epidemiological research links habitual cannabis smoking to several cancers but is complicated by small samples and co-occurring tobacco smoking. The authors then write that eating edibles does not seem to affect lung function or raise cancer risk, calling this a solid rationale for choosing this route as opposed to smoking cannabis, particularly for medical conditions such as cancer. No study of people who eat cannabis is cited for the last point.

Preparation of the manuscript was supported by RTI International internal funds and National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DA-03672. All eight authors are at RTI International. No conflict-of-interest statement is printed in the manuscript, and no cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are declared.

risk_of_bias.note: Chart review (Monte 2019): ROBINS-E overall high, with confounding, exposure measurement and selection each high (no adjustment for who took each form; route self-reported and presumed inhaled when not written down; everyone in the data attended an emergency department). Overview (Barrus 2016): a narrative review with no stated search or appraisal and second-hand figures, judged high overall.

inconsistency.note: One data set. The overview's statement that edibles account for most intoxication visits conflicts with the hospital count (115 of 762, 15.1%) but rests on a 2015 viewpoint that was not read, so it is shown as a contradicting anchor, not as a second data set.

indirectness.note: Worded for one Colorado hospital, 2012 to 2016, in an area of high cannabis availability. Route is edible against inhaled only (inhaled not split into flower, vaped oil or concentrates). The later and longer effect is cited from pharmacology work that was not read and was not measured in patients; the sales ratio uses assumed product contents.

imprecision.note: 238 edible visits; the intervals for the cardiovascular (1.4 to 8.4 points) and acute psychiatric (2.1 to 12.1) differences are wide for their size; eight symptom groups compared without correction; a dose charted in only 5.1% of visits.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with one data set.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). The claim rests on one chart review at one hospital and a narrative overview with no data of its own. Risk of bias -1: ROBINS-E overall high for the chart review (no adjustment; route self-reported and presumed inhaled when undocumented; every person in the data attended an emergency department); the overview has no stated search or appraisal and its figures are second-hand. Indirectness -1: one hospital in an area of high availability; edible against inhaled only; timing and the 11-OH-THC explanation come from pharmacology work that was not read and were not measured in patients; the sales ratio rests on assumed contents. Imprecision -1: 238 edible visits, wide intervals for two of the three findings that favour more events with edibles, no correction across eight symptom groups, a dose charted for 5.1% of visits. These downgrades together pass the floor, so the certainty is very low. Not downgraded for inconsistency or publication bias: one data set; the overview's statement that edibles account for most intoxication visits conflicts with the hospital count (15.1%) but rests on a viewpoint that was not read, so it is shown as a contradicting anchor and flagged. Worded as 'describes' rather than 'increases' or 'is associated with' because the data are shares of visits, not risks, with no count of people taking each form, and the claim combines counts, the authors' interpretation and second-hand pharmacology. The Discussion's causal wording and the 33-fold ratio are the authors' own reading and are reported as such, not adopted.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only, no advice. Rests on one chart review at one hospital (Monte 2019, the only primary study of route read for this claim) and a narrative overview (Barrus 2016: no stated search or appraisal; its timing, label-testing, child-poisoning and out-of-state figures are second-hand). Not yet readable and to be added: Tweet 2023 (child poisonings; the overview's child figures are second-hand and end in 2014 to 2015) and Vandrey 2015 (label accuracy; the overview's 83% is second-hand). The overview's statement that edibles account for most intoxication visits conflicts with the hospital count (115 of 762, 15.1%); its source, a 2015 viewpoint by the hospital group (Monte, Zane, Heard), was not read, and the conflict is shown as a contradicting anchor, not resolved. The editors' arithmetic (edible shares of visits by reason) needs recomputation by a second reader. Papers cited by these two (Kim 2016, Hall 2018, Wang 2014, Cao 2016, Grotenhermen 2003) were not read; the hospital group's papers are not independent of each other. Amounts, strengths and timings appear only as study conditions or as the sources describe them. Funding as printed: Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (Monte); RTI International internal funds and a NIDA grant (Barrus); no cannabis-industry funding is printed for either, so there is no industry-funded finding to pair. The Discussion's causal wording ('lead to') and the 33-fold ratio are the authors' reading; the claim does not adopt them.
